patterns.signal: You must restructure a function that has no tests and nobody can say what it is supposed to return
patterns.why: Record what the code does today, quirks included, so any behaviour change shows up as a red test. They pin current behaviour, not correct behaviour; fix quirks in a separate commit.

patterns.signal: A new rule must go into a tangled 600-line function and bolting it on feels risky
patterns.why: Make the change easy, then make the easy change: restructure first under green tests, then add the feature on top. Only worth it in code you are about to change anyway.

patterns.signal: A refactor step leaves several tests red and you cannot tell which edit caused it
patterns.why: One small structural change per run; green means commit, red means revert and take a smaller step. Feels slow, but you never debug a large broken diff.

patterns.signal: A single commit both restructures code and changes an output, and the reviewer cannot tell which part is the fix
patterns.why: A pure refactor should leave every test untouched, which makes it easy to review and bisect. Mixing them hides the behaviour change inside noise.

patterns.signal: You want to unit test logic that calls the database or the clock directly and cannot be isolated
patterns.why: Create a point where behaviour can be swapped without editing the call site, such as a parameter, interface or injected function. Adds indirection, so add seams only where tests need them.

patterns.signal: A long chain of `if type == ...` branches grows with every new variant and is copied in several places
patterns.why: Each variant owns its behaviour, so adding one means adding a class, not editing every switch. Overkill for two stable cases; a plain conditional is clearer there.

patterns.signal: A team ships a hard-coded shortcut to hit a launch date and someone asks whether that is acceptable
patterns.why: Debt is fine when it is known, written down and has a payoff plan, like a ticket with an owner. Unrecorded debt compounds silently until nobody knows it exists.

patterns.signal: The team has a long list of ugly modules and limited time to clean up
patterns.why: Pay down debt where change frequency times difficulty is highest; version-control history shows churn. Ugly code nobody touches costs nothing, so leave it.

patterns.signal: An agent's refactor diff edits existing test assertions so the suite goes green
patterns.why: Tell the agent tests must not change in a refactor; changed assertions mean the spec moved, not the structure. Review test files first and reject such diffs.

patterns.signal: CI broke overnight with no code change, after a dependency published a new patch release
patterns.why: The lockfile records exact transitive versions and hashes; `npm ci` or `uv sync --locked` fails instead of drifting. Applies to applications; libraries usually publish ranges, not locks.

patterns.signal: Dependencies are two years old and a single 'update everything' attempt broke dozens of tests
patterns.why: Bots like Dependabot or Renovate raise one small PR per update, each running the tests, so breakage is easy to attribute. Costs review time; batch low-risk patch bumps to limit noise.

patterns.signal: Builds must work offline or must survive a package being deleted from the public registry
patterns.why: Copying dependency source into the repo gives reproducible, auditable, offline builds. You then own patching and accept large diffs, so vendor only when availability or audit beats convenience.

patterns.signal: Someone wants to add a package to save ten lines of string padding
patterns.why: Every dependency is a trust decision and an update stream for its whole transitive tree. Small, stable helpers are cheaper to own than to import.

patterns.signal: A newly suggested package name looks almost right, is days old and has few downloads
patterns.why: Check name spelling, age, maintainers and download history to catch typosquatting and hallucinated names. A short cooldown on brand-new releases also blunts maintainer-takeover attacks.

patterns.signal: An internal package name like `acme-utils` could also be registered on the public registry
patterns.why: Route internal scopes only to your private registry so a higher public version cannot win resolution (dependency confusion). Requires registry config on every machine and in CI.

patterns.signal: A scanner reports 40 vulnerabilities and the team is tempted to ignore all alerts
patterns.why: Fix exploitable, exposed ones first; record why others are not reachable instead of muting them. A clean audit only means no known issues, not safety.

patterns.signal: Installing a package can run arbitrary code on developer machines and CI runners
patterns.why: Use `--ignore-scripts` or a package manager that blocks lifecycle scripts, and allowlist the few packages that genuinely need a build step. Some native packages then need manual setup.

patterns.signal: Security asks which services ship a given vulnerable library version and nobody can answer quickly
patterns.why: A software bill of materials lists every component and version per build, so exposure questions become a query. Only useful if generated automatically on each build and stored.

patterns.signal: Errors spiked minutes after a deploy and the cause is not yet understood
patterns.why: Restoring service beats understanding it; a five-minute rollback ends user pain while the evidence stays in logs. Not possible for irreversible data changes, so design migrations to be backward compatible.

patterns.signal: Several engineers are on the call, each debugging and restarting services independently
patterns.why: One person coordinates, decides and delegates but does not debug, keeping a single thread of control. Without one, conflicting changes make diagnosis impossible.

patterns.signal: The new code path is clearly the suspect and it is behind a toggle
patterns.why: Turning off a flag is faster and narrower than a full rollback. Only works if risky features ship behind flags and the off path is tested.

patterns.signal: Two responders each applied a fix at once and nobody knows which one helped
patterns.why: Change one thing, observe, then decide the next step, so cause and effect stay readable. Slower per step but avoids masking or compounding failures.

patterns.signal: After the outage nobody can reconstruct what was seen, decided and changed, or when
patterns.why: A scribe logs observations, decisions and actions with times; it becomes the postmortem timeline. Cheap to do live, nearly impossible to rebuild afterwards.

patterns.signal: Customers and support learn about the outage from social media rather than from you
patterns.use: Dedicated comms lead on a cadence
patterns.why: One person updates the status page and stakeholders on a fixed schedule, even with 'no news yet', so responders are not interrupted. Small teams double up, but someone must own it.

patterns.signal: A draft postmortem concludes that the engineer should have been more careful
patterns.why: Assume people acted sensibly with what they knew and ask why the system allowed the error. Blame hides information; system fixes like guardrails and checks prevent the repeat.

patterns.signal: Your 5 whys analysis ended at a single person and a single linear cause
patterns.why: Real failures have several conditions that combined; list them all instead of one chain. 5 whys is a useful prompt but stops wherever the investigator stops.

patterns.signal: The last three postmortems produced action items that were never done
patterns.why: Each action needs one owner, a due date and a verifiable outcome, tracked like other work. 'Be more careful' is not an action item.

patterns.signal: A teammate is sure the database is the bottleneck but nobody has profiled the slow page
patterns.why: Set a target such as p95 under 500 ms, profile, change one thing, re-measure. Intuition about bottlenecks is often wrong, and optimising the wrong thing is pure cost.

patterns.signal: A flame graph shows one wide box near the top of the stack for a single function
patterns.why: Width is share of samples, so wide boxes are where time goes; fix those and keep the rest readable. Micro-tuning code that takes 1% of time cannot help much.

patterns.signal: A list page issues one query for the list and then one more query per row
patterns.use: Fix N+1 with batching / eager load
patterns.why: Fetch related rows in one `IN (...)` query or a join, turning N+1 round trips into 1-2. Over-eager loading of data you do not show can be slower, so batch what is used.

patterns.signal: The same expensive result is recomputed on every request though its inputs rarely change
patterns.why: Trades memory and complexity for speed; decide up front how entries expire (TTL, invalidate on write, or accept staleness). A cache with no invalidation story returns wrong data.

patterns.signal: When a popular cache key expires, many requests hit the slow backend at the same instant
patterns.why: Let one request recompute while others wait or serve stale data, or add jittered expiry. Adds locking or background refresh logic, so use it only for hot keys.

patterns.signal: The average latency looks fine but users still complain the service is sometimes very slow
patterns.why: Averages hide tails; a p99 of 4 s hurts one request in a hundred, which is many users at scale. Percentiles need histograms, not just sums and counts.

patterns.signal: The profiler shows the CPU mostly idle while requests wait on network or disk
patterns.why: I/O-bound work needs batching, concurrency or fewer round trips; CPU-bound needs a better algorithm; memory-bound needs better data layout. The wrong class of fix does nothing.

patterns.signal: A microbenchmark shows a 10x speedup but end-to-end request latency did not change
patterns.why: Confirm gains in a realistic end-to-end metric with warm runs, production-sized data and repeated measurements. The micro win may be off the critical path, or eliminated as dead code.

patterns.signal: A loader reads millions of rows into memory just to show the first page
patterns.why: Skipping unneeded work usually beats making it faster. Pagination adds API complexity and stable ordering requirements, but bounds memory and latency.

patterns.signal: Someone proposes replacing a core component and nobody remembers why it was chosen
patterns.why: One short dated record per decision: context, options, decision, consequences. Supersede rather than edit, so history stays honest. Reserve ADRs for significant, costly-to-reverse choices.

patterns.signal: The on-call engineer gets an alert at 3 a.m. and does not know how to restart the worker safely
patterns.why: Exact commands, expected output, stop conditions and escalation, written for a tired stranger. Runbooks rot, so test them in drills and update after every incident.

patterns.signal: A new hire needs three days to get the project running because the steps live in one person's head
patterns.use: README tested on a clean machine
patterns.why: The README must say what it is and how to run, test and navigate it; every point where a newcomer gets stuck is a README bug. Keep it short and link out for depth.

patterns.signal: The wiki describes an API that changed six months ago and misleads readers confidently
patterns.why: Keep docs in the repo, reviewed in the same PR as the behaviour change and checked in CI (links, code samples). Wikis rot because nothing forces them to move with the code.

patterns.signal: A comment says `// increment i` while a surprising workaround nearby has no explanation
patterns.use: Comment the why, not the what
patterns.why: Code already shows what it does; comments earn their place by explaining intent, constraints and non-obvious choices. Restating the line is noise that drifts out of date.

patterns.signal: One document mixes a tutorial, a reference table and troubleshooting steps and serves none well
patterns.why: Learners, doers, lookers-up and understanders read differently, so separate the four kinds. More pages to maintain, but each is easier to find and keep correct.

patterns.signal: Only one engineer understands the billing integration and answers every question in chat
patterns.why: Move answers from chat into the repo and pair others on that area. Prioritise documenting what is hard to infer and costly to get wrong, not everything equally.

patterns.signal: An agent keeps guessing the test command and editing directories that are generated
patterns.why: A short repo file with build and test commands, conventions and no-go areas, loaded every session. Keep it accurate and brief; a stale one misleads agents just like stale docs mislead people.

patterns.signal: Leadership wants a full rewrite of a working twelve-year-old system that still makes money
patterns.why: Put a router in front and replace one capability at a time, redirecting its traffic; legacy shrinks until it can be switched off. Each step is shippable and reversible, but the router adds a hop.

patterns.signal: You must swap an internal library used in hundreds of call sites without a long-lived branch
patterns.why: Introduce an abstraction over the old implementation, move callers to it, build the new one behind it, then switch and delete the old. Trunk stays releasable; costs a temporary interface.

patterns.signal: A column must be renamed in a live database while old and new app versions run side by side
patterns.why: Add new structure, backfill, move reads, then remove the old once unused. Every step is backward compatible; it takes several deploys instead of one migration.

patterns.signal: You need confidence that the new service matches the old one on real production inputs
patterns.why: Send requests to both, return only the old response, and log differences. Real coverage without user risk, but side-effecting calls must be stubbed and it doubles load.

patterns.signal: Millions of existing rows must be converted while the system stays online
patterns.why: Process small batches that can be safely re-run after a crash, with progress checkpoints. Slower than one big UPDATE, but avoids long locks and partial, unrecoverable states.

patterns.signal: During a migration the app writes every change to both the old and the new store
patterns.why: Dual writes are not atomic, so stores drift. Keep one store authoritative and run a job that compares and repairs, or use change data capture to feed the other.

patterns.signal: The new implementation is ready and you are unsure it handles the long tail of real users
patterns.why: Route 1%, then 10%, then more, watching error and parity metrics, and keep a one-step switch back. Requires routing by user or request and both systems running for a while.

patterns.signal: A module looks unused but you are not certain nothing calls it
patterns.why: Search references, then add a usage counter or deprecation log and watch a full business cycle, including month-end jobs. Delete in a small separate commit; version control makes it reversible.

patterns.signal: A migration has been 'almost done' for a year and both systems still need patches
patterns.why: Track the end state, including shutting the old system off, as explicit owned work. Without it, the migration never finishes and you maintain two systems forever.

patterns.signal: An agent writes a confident call to a library method you have never seen
patterns.why: Models generate plausible continuations, not verified facts. Confirm with the compiler, a test or the installed source before trusting any function, flag or config key.

patterns.signal: The agent uses a library API that was renamed in a release after its training data
patterns.why: Knowledge stops at the training cutoff. Put the installed version number and the real docs or source in context, or let the agent read them, instead of relying on recall.

patterns.signal: An agent session that has run for hours starts ignoring an instruction given at the start
patterns.use: Compact or restart with a summary
patterns.why: Long contexts dilute attention and early content can be summarized away. Start fresh with a short summary and the key constraints, or put durable rules in an instruction file.

patterns.signal: A tool returns a 5,000-line log and the agent's next answer gets worse
patterns.use: Trim tool output to the signal
patterns.why: Everything in the window costs tokens, time and attention. Pass the failing assertion or a filtered excerpt; let the agent fetch more if it needs it.

patterns.signal: You run the same prompt twice at temperature 0 and get slightly different code
patterns.why: Even low temperature does not guarantee identical output across runs or backends. Check results with executable verification rather than expecting byte-identical generations.

patterns.signal: A task involves long numeric IDs, exact character counts or unusual identifiers and the model fumbles them
patterns.why: Tokenization splits rare strings unpredictably, so exact counting and copying are weak spots. Let code or a tool compute it, and let the model orchestrate.

patterns.signal: The model's answer sounds certain about a fact it has no way of knowing from context
patterns.why: Fluency is not a correctness signal; models have no built-in 'I do not know' alarm. Ask what observation or document backs the claim, and verify it.

patterns.signal: You are about to send 'fix the login bug' with no file, repro or definition of done
patterns.why: State the observable outcome, what is off limits, where to look, and a command that proves success. Takes a minute to write and prevents sprawling, unverifiable changes.

patterns.signal: You describe the desired style in adjectives and the output keeps missing it
patterns.use: Show an example (point at existing code)
patterns.why: Models imitate patterns in context very well; one concrete file or input-output pair beats a paragraph of description. Pick a good example: bad ones get copied just as faithfully.

patterns.signal: You repeat the same build command and conventions in every new session
patterns.why: Put recurring facts in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so they load automatically. It costs context every turn, so keep it short and remove lines that no longer match the code.

patterns.signal: The agent keeps re-adding a forbidden dependency despite chat reminders across sessions
patterns.use: Fix the instructions, not the chat
patterns.why: Corrections in chat vanish at the next session; update the instruction file or spec so they persist. Add a mechanical check like a lint rule where the rule really matters.

patterns.signal: A feature spans several sessions and a fresh agent keeps losing the thread
patterns.why: Problem, non-goals, interface, acceptance criteria and open questions in the repo survive session resets and let any agent resume. Overhead is not worth it for a one-line fix.

patterns.signal: The prompt has grown to include whole logs, unrelated files and old contradictory rules
patterns.why: Irrelevant tokens dilute attention and raise cost. Include what the task needs, link to the rest, and let the agent read files on demand.

patterns.signal: One prompt asks for a bug fix, a refactor and new docs at once
patterns.why: Unrelated goals compete for attention and produce one tangled diff. Separate tasks are easier to verify and to revert individually.

patterns.signal: A conversation is full of failed attempts and you keep arguing with the agent to change course
patterns.why: Failed attempts stay in context and steer the model back toward them. A fresh session with a sharper prompt and what you learned is usually faster.

patterns.signal: The agent claims the tests pass but the transcript shows no test command was run
patterns.why: The model only knows what tool results it saw. Ask which file it read or command it ran, and give it a runnable check so its loop gets ground truth.

patterns.signal: You are designing a tool and the model keeps calling it with wrong or missing arguments
patterns.why: A clear name, a description of when to use it, and a tight parameter schema guide correct calls. Few focused tools beat one do-everything tool with free-text input.

patterns.signal: A tool returns huge raw output that floods the agent's context on every call
patterns.use: Tool returns a concise, structured result
patterns.why: Return failures, counts and pointers rather than full dumps, with a way to page for more. Keeps context for reasoning, at the cost of hiding detail the agent must explicitly request.

patterns.signal: Searching a huge codebase fills the main context with file listings before real work starts
patterns.why: A separate loop with its own context does the search and returns only a summary; also enables parallel work. The summary can drop details, so ask for file paths and evidence.

patterns.signal: The transcript shows the same failing command run five times in a row
patterns.use: Step limit + interrupt with a new hint
patterns.why: Repeated identical calls mean the agent is stuck. Cap iterations and intervene with new information instead of letting it burn tokens retrying.

patterns.signal: You approve every read prompt without looking, and a risky shell command slips through too
patterns.why: Allow reads by default, scope edits to a directory, allowlist safe shell patterns, and gate the rest. Fewer prompts means the ones left get real attention.

patterns.signal: Ten MCP servers are connected and the agent picks odd tools while context fills with tool definitions
patterns.use: Enable only the tools the task needs
patterns.why: Every tool definition consumes context and widens the attack surface. Connect integrations per project or task, not globally.

patterns.signal: Long sessions cost far more than expected and each step is slow
patterns.use: Prompt caching + cheaper model for chores
patterns.why: Each loop iteration resends context; caching cuts repeated-prefix cost, and smaller models handle mechanical subtasks. Keep review and judgment on the stronger model.

patterns.signal: A task touches several files or an unfamiliar area and the agent wants to start coding immediately
patterns.why: Read first, agree a plan, then build in steps and check each. A wrong early decision is cheap to fix in a ten-line plan and expensive in a finished diff.

patterns.signal: You want to review the approach before any file is touched
patterns.why: The agent investigates and proposes files, steps and tests without editing. Cheapest review you will do; skip it for trivial, single-line changes.

patterns.signal: An agent produced a 1,800-line diff across 35 files that you cannot meaningfully review
patterns.why: Ask for one logical change at a time and commit after each green step. If you cannot read the diff, you are not supervising it; split or redo it.

patterns.signal: Two agents must work at the same time on separate bugs in the same repository
patterns.why: Each agent gets its own checkout and branch, so they cannot overwrite each other. Only pays off for independent tasks; overlapping files mean merge conflicts.

patterns.signal: The agent has failed the same way three times despite rephrased prompts
patterns.why: More prompting rarely fixes a repeated failure. Write the tricky part yourself or start fresh with a summary; also take over when the change needs unwritten judgment.

patterns.signal: The diff includes 'while I was there' cleanups in files unrelated to the task
patterns.why: Unrequested edits hide risk and bloat review. State scope up front and send the extras back as separate tasks if they are worth doing.

patterns.signal: An agent session runs long with no checkpoints and you cannot tell what is done
patterns.why: Ask it to stop after each step, run the tests and report what it did not verify. Slightly slower, but each step is reviewable and revertable.

patterns.signal: A bug report arrives and the agent proposes a fix without reproducing it
patterns.why: Write a test that reproduces the bug and watch it fail, then fix. Proves the test can detect the problem; a test that never failed may test nothing.

patterns.signal: The agent says 'all tests pass' and the same diff changed a failing test's expected value
patterns.why: A changed assertion means the spec moved, not the code. Read test-file changes before anything else and require a stated reason for every weakened or deleted test.

patterns.signal: A summary from the agent says 'verified' with no command or output shown
patterns.why: Require the exact command and its real output. The model's opinion of its own work is not evidence; an executed, independent check is.

patterns.signal: Code compiles and passes the happy-path test, but involves pagination, dates or ranges
patterns.why: Off-by-ones, timezone assumptions and 0- vs 1-based indexes pass typical inputs. Test empty, single, last and just-past-limit cases explicitly.

patterns.signal: Your product calls an LLM and you judge prompt changes by trying three demo inputs
patterns.why: A repeatable set of realistic and adversarial cases with exact, programmatic or rubric scoring. Cherry-picked demos hide regressions; evals catch them before users do.

patterns.signal: You tuned a prompt until all 20 of your example cases pass
patterns.why: Cases used for tuning measure overfitting, not quality. Keep a separate set you never tune on, and grow it from real failures.

patterns.signal: Outputs are open-ended text and exact-match scoring is impossible
patterns.why: A judge model scores against a rubric at scale, but it has biases. Calibrate against human labels on a sample and treat scores as relative, not absolute truth.

patterns.signal: Overall eval accuracy is steady but one category of users reports more failures
patterns.why: Averages hide drops in one slice and rare severe failures. Report accuracy per category and track must-never-happen cases separately.

patterns.signal: An agent will read issues, web pages or dependency docs written by people outside your team
patterns.why: Models cannot reliably separate instructions from data, so injected text can steer actions. Assume it is hostile and limit what the agent can do while reading it.

patterns.signal: One agent session has secrets, reads untrusted content and can make network requests
patterns.why: Private data, untrusted input and external communication together enable exfiltration. Remove any one leg, e.g. no secrets in reach or no egress, instead of relying on detection.

patterns.signal: An agent needs to run arbitrary shell commands and install packages to finish a task
patterns.why: Run it in a container or VM with a disposable checkout and network limited to the registry and git host. A successful injection then cannot reach beyond the box.

patterns.signal: An agent that only reads staging logs is running with your personal admin cloud profile
patterns.why: Give a read-only, scoped token for that task and environment. Limits blast radius if the agent is tricked or wrong; costs a little setup per role.

patterns.signal: The agent is about to drop a table, force-push, delete cloud resources or send email
patterns.why: Gate destructive actions on explicit approval that shows the real command and target, not a model-written summary. Prefer reversible designs like branches and soft deletes.

patterns.signal: `.env` and SSH keys sit in the directory the agent can read
patterns.why: Deny-list secret paths in the agent's settings and keep secrets out of prompts, instruction files and code. Anything in context can be echoed or exfiltrated.

patterns.signal: A teammate wants to connect a third-party MCP server they found online
patterns.why: An MCP server runs with your permissions and its outputs enter context. Review source and publisher, pin versions, and scope its access like any other dependency.

patterns.signal: Generated code adds a new network call, shell execution or string-built SQL query
patterns.why: Agents reproduce classic vulnerabilities like injection and missing authorization checks. Scan diffs for new egress, exec, query building and auth changes.

patterns.signal: The only test suite takes 40 minutes and needs a live database, so the agent skips it
patterns.why: A tier that runs in seconds without external services lets the agent verify after every change. Keep slower integration tests too, but run them less often.

patterns.signal: Tests fail intermittently and the agent is told to just rerun them
patterns.why: Flaky tests teach the agent that red means nothing, so real failures get ignored. Fix the nondeterminism or isolate the test until fixed.

patterns.signal: A function calls the system clock or random directly and its tests depend on when they run
patterns.why: Pass a clock, seed or client as a dependency so tests control them and become deterministic. Adds a parameter or interface; worth it on logic that matters.

patterns.signal: Setup, test and lint each need a different multi-step incantation from a wiki page
patterns.why: A Makefile or task runner with `setup`, `test`, `lint`, `check` removes guesswork for humans and agents and shrinks the instruction file. Keep `check` identical to what CI runs.

patterns.signal: The agent keeps passing a bare number where an amount with a currency is expected
patterns.why: Types and schemas (OpenAPI, JSON Schema, protobuf) reject a whole class of mistakes before any test runs. Costs some annotation; most valuable at module and system edges.

patterns.signal: A 5,000-line file mixes unrelated responsibilities and edits keep breaking distant code
patterns.why: One responsibility per module and no hidden globals or import-time side effects keep edits local and files within comfortable context size. Over-splitting adds navigation cost.

patterns.signal: The agent keeps hand-editing files that are regenerated by a code generator
patterns.why: Put generated output in a clearly named directory with a header, document the regen command, and add a CI check that fails on manual edits. Stops repeated wasted work.

patterns.signal: A test failure prints only `AssertionError` with no values
patterns.why: Expected versus actual values let the agent, and you, fix the problem from one run instead of guessing. Use assertion helpers that print diffs.

patterns.signal: The agent stumbles on the same thing in repo after repo, e.g. cannot find the test command
patterns.use: Treat agent stumbles as codebase bugs
patterns.why: Each repeated stumble points at a missing script, doc line or guard. Fixing it once makes every future task, by agents or new hires, cheaper and safer.
